Question: Why do I feel like I'm getting worse and worse after 3 cold turkey months of taking Effexor for 13 and a half years when the first month I seemed to be almost cured?
Answer: Recovery is a process. While some patients experience an onset of post-discontinuation symptoms and then those symptoms all collectively fade over time, many patients experience new symptoms arising long after others first did, and many people experience symptoms that come and go in waves, sometimes over and over again for months or years. The bottom line is the recovery is a process rather than a simple forward progression away from symptoms. Some symptoms may newly appear or worsen over time, some may cycle on and off periodically, some may morph into something else. After more than a decade on drugs, you can anticipate there being more difficulties ahead, this is not something people can usually quit overnight and then feel recovered from within days or weeks or even a few months. The body is trying to restabilize and to address any underlying problems drug use had caused besides just physical dependence (deficiencies, damages, downregulation, and so forth). There is more to recovering from long-term psychiatric drug use than just getting through the withdrawal symptoms, and for some people all the other stuff involved can actually be more taxing or confusing than withdrawal itself. It is not unusual for someone to have months or even years of worsening symptoms after more than a few years of continuous drug use. More than a decade of use should be taken as a giant “caution” sign to take steps slowly. People with a history of severe stress on the nervous system, which you mention in your post, are also more likely to struggle with recovery as a result. Cold turkeying is bad news in general, and can potentially alter the course and severity of withdrawal. It can also make it more difficult for someone to transition away from daily drug use. Dysfunction, disorientation, and impairment are typical, not strange or uncommon. After use as long as you mention, patients often require specialized consultation so that they can properly prepare themselves for the journey and have the resources and support to work through the months or years of struggle. Skipping a gradual taper was likely a very bad idea, though it may be possible to reinstate a partial dose to see if it alleviates your symptoms at all. Read places like Surviving Antidepressants and discuss your options with your doctors: Important topics in the Tapering forum and FAQ

Question: Is depersonalization and derealization a side effect of Lexapro?
Answer: Dissociation is a risk of all drugs like escitalopram, yes. SSRIs, including Lexapro, and most any other psychiatric drugs can cause dissociation, both as an effect of actively using the drug and as a reduction-emergent effect. This includes depersonalization, derealization, and other forms of dissociation. Some kinds of reactions will be more common than others, and how often dissociation happens can also depend on factors like the dose, duration of use, management strategies (most importantly tapering speed), someone’s health, any other drugs being used, someone’s propensity to dissociate, and so on. Patients with a history of dissociation should be cautious with psychotropic drugs in general, but since there are differing causes for dissociation, stressors that are triggers for one person may not be so for another, or may even reduce the incidence of dissociation (for instance if strong emotions are a trigger for someone and a drug is emotionally blunting). No special medical or psychological history is required to experience dissociation with an SSRI, nor is any predisposition implied by that kind of reaction. It is not a rare effect of drug use or drug discontinuation, but is not guaranteed to happen by any stretch, either, even if someone is more susceptible.

Question: I am so obsessed with trying to figure out what's wrong with me (mental health / diagnosis-wise). I think some of my symptoms are actually severe, but I could be exaggerating. How have you managed to get a decent perspective on your mental health?
Answer: Here’s the thing: YOU get to decide what matters. It isn’t about something being right with you or wrong with you, or difficulties being considered mild or severe, or something qualifying for one diagnosis or another or no diagnosis at all. None of that determines your own goals and priorities and whether you’d like one or more things in your life to be different. How common something is, whether other random strangers relate, what a clinician would say…those are all superficial in nature. What really matters is who you want to be and what you think matters. If there are things you’d like to be different, you can explore how to make changes or how to evaluate whether those downsides come with upsides you feel are a fair tradeoff. Psychiatric diagnoses are literally just bullshit. They don’t explain anything about what is going on with you, or what your needs might be, or how to constructively address anything going on. They aren’t a part of figuring anything out because they don’t bring any new information or insight to the table. Your experiences and beliefs and behaviors are the same no matter what label an industry applies to them, and applying a label does not provide anything to your understanding the experiences, beliefs, and behaviors themselves did not already. A decent perspective on these things is to embrace that your experiences matter, that psychiatric labeling is not a way to understand them or determine what your values are, and that if you are struggling, there are things which can be done to promote positive change. Honesty is important: being willing to confront our emotions, our needs, our behaviors, and the patterns in those things which require understanding for us to more capably create a better life for ourselves. Appropriately assigning causality is important: discerning what factors are producing the outcomes you desire, or the outcomes you wish to avoid, so you can respond to those factors constructively. Marketing mythology and industry acceptance is neither required nor necessarily even a helpful rather than counterproductive influence. It is normal to crave understanding, validation, agency, and to seek those things. But, some manners of seeking them will be more productive or less dangerous than others. Question: What are the risks of not being honest with a psychiatrist about your mental health issues?
Answer: If you want something, you may not get it. Good advice depends on good information. If a practitioner is not provided good, accurate, adequately detailed information, their input and management can suffer greatly as a result, even if they are a good psychiatrist. This question can read a bit like asking what the risks are of screwing up the guidance system for an intercontinental nuclear missile. Psychiatry is already dangerous enough when everyone is honest and acting aboveboard. That said, most psychiatrists are not very good psychiatrists and will either rather often do a poor job even with good information or will use correct information against you instead of for you. Being selective about what you share is essential when dealing with medical professionals, because your wellbeing and your life are at risk from them, but sharing too little or lying when correct and complete information is necessary for you to get what you want from the consultation can be pointless at best or deadly at worst. The ideal is to find a practitioner who earns your trust and accountably acts in your interest. There is such a thing as a doctor who helps, including some psychiatrists. Patients who don’t have that luxury are stuck with deciding what to share, how, and when in order to both protect themselves from bad physician behavior and ideas and to still work on what they want to with their clinician. Before making these kinds of decisions, I strongly recommend educating about psychiatry, psychiatric dogma, and patient outcomes.

Question: I ran out of Venlafaxine, can I substitute with fluoxetine?
Answer: Learn and weigh your options. If you have been using venlafaxine for more than 1–2 months and you will not be having access to it or to other prescribing for at least another 1–2 months, it might be worth considering a cold swap to fluoxetine if the alternative is an unmitigated cold turkeying of SRIs in general. This carries its own risks and is something to discuss with a pharmacist if you’re not able to talk with your prescriber. However, if you’re just missing a couple of days between refills or plan to get a new prescription within the next week or two, adding fluoxetine may likely be more problematic than helpful, as it can be upsetting and also has a long half-life that can interfere with your reinstating venlafaxine when you have it again. There is no perfect or one-size-fits-all answer here and you have to consider the details of your situation, your history of drug reactions, and your access to resources. On one hand, venlafaxine and fluoxetine are actually a bit more cross-compatible than most SRI drugs and fluoxetine is the gold standard tapering SRI, but on the other hand, none of these drugs are truly interchangeable and whether or not you experience problems swapping them or starting a new drug in general is more personal and variable. There is also the concern of drug usefulness — my answer so far has focused on minimizing withdrawal phenomena, but a drug being helpful to you brings a whole different set of concerns. If you find venlafaxine useful, that does not necessarily mean you will find any other drug useful. If you’ve been on fluoxetine in the past, which may be the case if you have a stock around, that is a decent gauge of its potential but you may or may not respond in the same way when going back to it, especially if you just cold turkeying venlafaxine. If your question is just whether these two drugs are fair substitutes for one another, the answer is no. The pharmacology is a lot more complex than that, and even switching between release designs or manufacturers of the same drug can cause problems for some patients. Whether swapping for fluoxetine is your best risk-reducing measures in the moment, though, depends on more than just that. I strongly recommend getting in contact with your professionals to see what options they have in mind and what their recommendations are. Remember that professions can still give bad, harmful advice so you should research additionally before making a decision instead of following their advice blindly. And, as mentioned, if you can’t see your prescriber and can’t see another doctor, at least speak with a pharmacist, which is free and doesn’t require an appointment in places like the US.
